name: Intense pulsed light (IPL photofacial)

card.summary: A broad-spectrum flashlamp treatment used in clinics for sun spots, redness and thread veins, and also sold as home hair-removal devices.
card.note: Hyperpigmentation is the main reported complication, and IPL has been reported to worsen melasma.

quick.overview:
Intense pulsed light is a handheld flashlamp that fires broad-spectrum light into the skin, and the photofacial is its cosmetic skin-rejuvenation use. Clinics offer it for pigmentation, sun damage and visible small vessels, and the same technology is used in some hair-removal systems.

Publicly accessible sources give limited trial detail for the facial uses; the technology is better documented for vascular lesions and hair reduction.
quick.mechanism: A xenon lamp emits light of roughly 400 to 1,200 nanometres. Filters remove the most damaging ultraviolet and the longest infrared wavelengths, and the remaining light is absorbed by melanin, haemoglobin and water, heating the targets. Interchangeable filters let one device address different conditions.
quick.risks: Reported complications include temporary side effects and hyperpigmentation. Photosensitising medicines and skin damage are listed as contraindications. IPL has been reported to worsen melasma, and rules for devices and operators vary by jurisdiction.

lead: Intense pulsed light (IPL) is a skin-treatment technology in which a computer-controlled xenon flashlamp emits pulses of broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1,200 nanometres, through filters that remove much ultraviolet and long infrared light.[1] Unlike single-wavelength lasers, it can be tuned for different targets using interchangeable filters.[1]

The cosmetic application usually called a photofacial or photorejuvenation targets pigmentation, sun damage and thread veins. IPL was first developed for vascular conditions, and it is also used for hair removal, rosacea, acne and dry-eye disease linked to meibomian gland dysfunction.[1]
Pigmented lesions are among the main appearance uses, though encyclopedic sources describe the evidence base as relying on primary studies that used differing devices.[1]
infobox: Vascular lesions 1995, pigmented lesions 1996, hair removal 1997[1]

paras: Light pulses are absorbed by chromophores, mainly melanin, haemoglobin and water, which heat and are damaged. Pigmented spots absorb the melanin-targeted wavelengths, and vessels absorb the haemoglobin-targeted wavelengths.[1]

Shimon Eckhouse invented IPL in 1992 and filed the detailed patent that was granted in 1995. ESC Medical commercialised the technology, and FDA clearances followed for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.[1]

Photorejuvenation targets pigmentation, sun damage and thread veins, and the technology is also described as used for photoaging, melasma, rosacea and actinic keratosis. Encyclopedic sources state it is at least as effective as pulsed dye lasers for vascular conditions.[1]
Melasma is a special case: a separate reference on that condition notes that IPL may worsen it.[2]

For hair removal, a 2006 comparison cited in encyclopedic sources found no significant difference in six-month hair reduction among alexandrite lasers (68.75 percent), diode lasers (71.71 percent) and IPL (66.96 percent); side effects were 9.5, 28.9 and 15.3 percent respectively and all temporary. Other statements in the same source describe IPL as less effective than laser for hair removal while noting patient satisfaction.[1]
Hair removal results are described as a permanent reduction rather than total removal, and only active follicles respond.[1]

Hyperpigmentation is the main complication noted. Photosensitising medicines and damaged skin are listed as contraindications, and one manufacturer says the device suits light to medium skin tones.[1]
Regulation varies by jurisdiction, and a loose split between beauty-grade and medical-grade devices has been described, including home devices for hair removal.[1]
No studies found for the photofacial in a looksmaxxing context. Related research on IPL covers hair removal, where a 2006 comparison with alexandrite and diode lasers is described above.[1]

timeline.event: US patent granted; FDA clearance for vascular lesions.[1]
